Enter your current balance, monthly contributions, expected return, and years until retirement. The calculator above will show your retirement savings and break down how much comes from growth versus your own deposits. Use it to see how small changes today can shape your future nest egg. $1,540,606 savings at retirement $5,135 monthly income (4% rule) $1,184,606 investment growth Share Interactive — edit any field What a Market Drop Does to Your 401(k) Balance A 10% to 20% drop leaves 80% to 90% of your 401(k) balance and requires an 11.11% to 25.00% gain to recover. In our internal modeling, we applied 10%, 20% and 30% drops to a hypothetical $100,000 balance and worked out the gain each one needs to recover. Because losses shrink your starting base, recovery follows the formula d / (1 - d) and demands a larger percentage gain. Market Drop Balance After Gain Needed to Recover Years to Recover at 7% 10% $90,000 11.11% About 1.6 years 20% $80,000 25.00% About 3.3 years 30% $70,000 42.86% About 5.3 years These recovery estimates assume a hypothetical $100,000 balance and the calculator's default 7% yearly return without new contributions, fees, taxes, or inflation, whereas real annual returns fluctuate. Turbulent market guidance from the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority (FINRA) lists five steps for turbulent markets, and you cannot control market swings. Four bear on whether to sell: FINRA advises clarifying your financial goals and tying them to your long-term plan. FINRA recommends diversifying across and within asset classes to prevent overexposure to any single investment, sector, or asset category. FINRA suggests avoiding impulsive moves during volatile periods and focusing on your future. FINRA notes that dollar-cost averaging by investing a fixed amount on a regular schedule can reduce emotional decision-making. FINRA advises working only with registered professionals, which you can check with BrokerCheck , and being wary of guaranteed risk-free returns. Based on our internal modeling, drops of 10% to 30% are arithmetically recoverable if a long time horizon gives your portfolio room to rebound. If you need the money within two years, a 20% drop (about 3.3 years to recover at 7%) or a 30% drop (about 5.3 years) may not recover in time. If you keep contributing, new deposits buy shares at lower prices, which can shorten recovery. This page offers general information and cannot judge your time horizon or goals. Whether to sell depends on your time horizon and goals. With many years until you need the money, a drop is recoverable; if you need withdrawals within a few years or hold mostly one asset, see how to choose a financial advisor . Enter your own balance in the calculator above, then see the portfolio rebalancing calculator to check how your mix of investments looks. How it's calculated The 401k calculator grows your current balance and monthly contributions forward to your retirement age. It assumes a fixed annual return that compounds each year. You enter your starting balance, monthly contribution (including any employer match), expected yearly return, and target retirement age. The tool then splits your final balance into two parts: the money you put in and the investment growth on top. This split reveals the power of compounding. Real markets rise and fall, so treat the result as a planning estimate, not a guarantee. To plan beyond your workplace plan, see the retirement savings calculator . One detail most 401(k) planning tools skip: your 401(k) is part of your taxable estate at death. If your projected balance plus other assets is anywhere near the 2026 federal $15M exemption (permanent under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, P.L. 119-21) or any state estate tax threshold — Oregon starts at $1M, Massachusetts at $2M, Washington at $3M — the estate tax bill can be meaningful. The estate tax calculator shows your federal + state exposure using 2026 numbers. And critically, the beneficiary designation on the 401(k) OVERRIDES anything your will or trust says, so keep it current and consistent with your estate plan. See our 401(k) beneficiary rules guide for exactly what happens to the account, and to your beneficiary's tax bill, when you die. A worked example Say you are 30 years old with $20,000 already in your 401(k). You contribute $800 per month, including your employer match, and expect a 7% annual return until you retire at 65. The calculator projects $1,540,606 in savings at retirement. Your $20,000 starting balance plus $336,000 in contributions over 35 years make up the money you put in, while investment growth adds $1,184,606. Using the 4% rule, that balance could provide about $5,135 per month in your first year of retirement. Common mistakes to avoid Skipping the full employer match. The match is free money and an instant return on your contribution. Always contribute enough to capture every matching dollar your employer offers. Forgetting to include the employer match in your monthly contribution figure. The calculator expects your total monthly deposit, so add your share plus your employer's. Setting an unrealistic return rate. A fixed 7% is a common long-term stock estimate, but higher numbers can badly overstate your balance. Waiting too long to start. Starting at 30 instead of 40 gives your money an extra decade to compound, which often doubles the final result. Ignoring the 2026 contribution limit. You can defer up to $24,500 in 2026, plus an $8,000 catch-up if you are age 50 or older. Frequently asked questions What is a 401(k)? A 401(k) is an employer-sponsored retirement account that lets you contribute part of your paycheck before it's taxed (traditional) or after it's taxed with tax-free withdrawals later (Roth), and invest those contributions for growth until retirement. Many employers match a portion of what you contribute, and the IRS sets annual limits on how much you can defer — $24,500 in 2026, plus an $8,000 catch-up if you're 50 or older. Use the calculator above to project how your own balance could grow. What does a 401k calculator do? A 401k calculator projects how much your 401(k) will grow by retirement. You enter your balance, monthly contributions, expected return, and retirement age. It then estimates your final savings and shows how much comes from growth versus your own deposits. How much can I contribute to a 401(k) in 2026? You can contribute up to $24,500 to your 401(k) in 2026. If you are age 50 or older, you can add an $8,000 catch-up contribution, for a total of $32,500. These limits apply to your own deferrals, not employer matching. For next year's figure, see the 2027 401(k) contribution limits . Does the calculator include my employer match? Yes, if you include the match in your monthly contribution. Enter your total monthly deposit, combining your own contribution and your employer's match. The employer match is essentially free money, so contribute enough to earn the full amount offered. How much does an employer match add over a career? The impact is substantial. On a $50,000 salary with a 3% employer match, your employer contributes $1,500 per year. At a 7% annual return over 30 years, that $1,500 annual match alone grows to approximately $141,700 — without you contributing a single extra dollar. The match is also an instant 100% return on the dollars that trigger it, which is why always contributing enough to capture the full match is the highest-priority step in retirement planning. To model the combined effect of your contributions and the match, include both amounts in the monthly contribution field above, then compare the full projection in the retirement savings calculator . What return rate should I use? Many planners use a fixed 7% annual return as a long-term stock market estimate. The calculator assumes this rate stays the same every year. Real returns vary, so treat the projection as an estimate and try a few different rates. What if I withdraw from my 401(k) early? Withdrawing before age 59½ usually costs a 10% penalty plus income tax, and it erases future growth. Estimate the damage first with our 401k early withdrawal calculator before cashing out. Can I use this calculator if I'm self-employed? You can use it to project savings growth, but a workplace 401(k)'s $24,500 employee deferral limit doesn't reflect a self-employed saver's options. A solo 401(k) lets you contribute as both employee and employer, and a SEP-IRA has its own separate limit — see our SEP-IRA vs. solo 401(k) comparison for which fits your situation. Should I sell my 401(k) when the market drops? Deciding whether to sell depends on your time horizon and goals, though this page cannot judge your individual situation. The Financial Industry Regulatory Authority (FINRA) advises investors to clarify goals tied to a long-term plan, diversify across and within asset classes, and avoid impulsive moves in volatile markets. FINRA also notes that dollar-cost averaging can reduce emotional decision-making. How much does my 401(k) need to gain to recover from a 20% drop? Your balance needs a 25.00% gain to recover from a 20% drop. A 20% drop from a hypothetical $100,000 balance leaves $80,000, which takes about 3.3 years to recover at a constant 7% return assuming no ongoing contributions, fees, taxes, or inflation. Real returns vary. Not legal advice This page gives general educational information, not personalized investment advice. Enter your starting balance, APR, cycle length and 365- or 360-day basis in the calculator above. You can also add a payment made during the cycle and the day it posts. The calculator then shows the daily periodic rate, the average daily balance, the yearly cost if the balance stays flat, and the effective annual rate with daily compounding. For example, take a $5,000 balance at 24% APR with no payment during the cycle. The cycle runs 30 days, and the daily rate uses a 365-day year. That gives a daily rate of 0.0658%, an average daily balance of $5,000, and interest of $98.63 for the cycle. If a $1,000 payment posts on day 11, interest for the same cycle drops to $85.48. That payment saves $13.15 compared with paying nothing during the cycle. Share Interactive — edit any field 10% APR Cap Scenario No 10% credit card interest cap is law today; S.381 and H.R.1944 are proposals. Per the Congressional Research Service (CRS) report updated March 10, 2026 and the text of S.381 on govinfo , S.381 and H.R.1944 are proposals in the 119th Congress that would cap credit card annual percentage rates (APRs) at 10% until January 1, 2031. S.381 was introduced February 4, 2025 and referred to the Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs, and committee status after those records is not confirmed here. In our internal modeling, we compared one billing cycle at 24% and at 10% on the $5,000 example used above. APR One 30-Day Cycle One Year, Flat Balance 24% $98.63 $1,200.00 10% $41.10 $500.00 Difference $57.53 $700.00 These numbers assume simple interest on a flat $5,000 balance, a 30-day cycle in a 365-day year, no payments made during the cycle, no new fees added, and the card staying open at 10%. To evaluate your current rate against common ranges, read our guide on what counts as a good APR for a credit card . The CRS report describes several practical tradeoffs if a cap takes effect: * Access to credit from traditional sources could be affected. * Banks may choose to limit credit products or add auxiliary fees. * Borrowers may shift to higher-APR sources outside banking. * Some economists state that reduced credit availability could benefit some consumers. A single new fee of $57.53 or more per cycle would wipe out the entire monthly interest savings on this $5,000 balance, and losing access to an existing card line could cost more than the rate reduction saves. Based on our internal modeling, a cardholder who keeps a $5,000 balance at 10% with no added charges would save about $57.53 per 30-day cycle. The saving depends on the final bill language and on how card issuers respond. S.381 as introduced, in section 107(f)(2), bars fees used to evade the cap and limits non-finance-charge fees to finance charges assessed. CRS also notes that cardholders who still revolve a balance at the lower APR could benefit. Per CRS, the proposed limits apply generally to consumer cards rather than business credit lines. This scenario does not apply to anyone who pays their full statement balance each month, because carrying no balance generates zero interest charges. Passage of a federal bill with altered caps, different fee rules, or another expiration date would change these numbers. Enter your current balance and rate in the calculator above, or plan a zero-balance target with our credit card payoff calculator . How it works The daily periodic rate is your APR divided by the number of days in the year your card issuer uses. At 24% APR on a 365-day year, the daily rate is 0.0658%. Some issuers divide by 360 instead, which raises the daily rate to 0.0667%. On the same $5,000 balance, that lifts one cycle's interest from $98.63 to $100.00. Set the day-count input to match the basis printed on your statement. The average daily balance is the average of each day's balance across the billing cycle. The calculator uses the full balance until your payment posts and the reduced balance from that day on. Take the same $5,000 balance with a $1,000 payment that posts on day 11 of the cycle. The balance sits at $5,000 for the first 10 days. It sits at $4,000 for the remaining 20 days, which averages out to $4,333.33. Every day after the payment counts at the lower balance, so the same payment posted earlier in the cycle pulls the average down further. Interest for the cycle equals the average daily balance times the daily rate times the days in the cycle. With no payment, the average daily balance stays at $5,000 and the daily rate is 0.0658%. Over 30 days, that comes to $98.63. With the day-11 payment, the same math on $4,333.33 gives $85.48. The calculator reports the $13.15 difference as the interest that payment saves. The calculator also shows what your APR costs over a full year if the balance stays flat. Held flat for a year, the $5,000 balance costs $1,200 in simple interest. When interest compounds daily, each day's interest joins the balance and is charged interest itself. The effective annual rate then works out to 27.11%, above the 24% APR. The formula is one plus the daily rate, raised to the power of the days in the year, minus one. The calculator covers purchase interest only. It leaves out any grace period, fees, cash advances and new purchases. Issuers also differ in how they compound within a cycle and how they round, so your statement can come in slightly off the figure above. Use the APR, cycle length and day-count basis shown on your statement, since the defaults in the calculator are placeholders. To pay a balance down, use the credit card payoff calculator . To judge the rate itself, read what counts as a good APR for a credit card . Frequently asked questions How do I calculate my credit card interest? Divide your APR by the days in the year to get the daily rate, multiply it by your average daily balance, then multiply by the days in the billing cycle. Take a $5,000 balance at 24% APR. Over a 30-day cycle on a 365-day year, it is charged $98.63. Enter the figures from your own statement in the calculator above to get your number. How much interest will a $5,000 balance cost in a month? At 24% APR, a $5,000 balance is charged $98.63 in one billing cycle. That assumes a 30-day cycle, a 365-day year and no payment during the cycle. On a 360-day basis, the same cycle costs $100.00. A different APR changes the figure, so enter your own rate above. What is the daily periodic rate? The daily periodic rate is your APR divided by the days in the year. At 24% APR on a 365-day year, it is 0.0658% a day. On a 360-day year, the same APR gives 0.0667% a day. What is the average daily balance? The average daily balance is the average of each day's balance across the billing cycle. A payment lowers it from the day the payment posts. Start with $5,000 and post a $1,000 payment on day 11. Across a 30-day cycle, the balance averages $4,333.33. Does paying early in the billing cycle lower my interest? Yes. A payment lowers the balance for every remaining day in the cycle, so an earlier payment means a lower average daily balance. On a $5,000 balance at 24% APR, a $1,000 payment posting on day 11 drops the cycle's interest to $85.48. That is $13.15 less than the $98.63 charged with no payment. Why is the effective annual rate higher than my APR? When interest compounds daily, each day's interest is added to the balance and then charged interest itself. At 24% APR, daily compounding over a 365-day year gives an effective annual rate of 27.11%. Simple interest on a flat $5,000 balance comes to $1,200 for the year. Why does my statement show a slightly different amount? Some issuers divide the APR by 365 days and some by 360. On the $5,000 example, that difference is $98.63 versus $100.00 for one cycle. Issuers also differ in how they compound within a cycle and how they round, which can shift the statement amount slightly. Set the day-count input to the basis on your statement to get closer. Does this calculator include a grace period or fees? No. It covers purchase interest only, with no grace period, fees, cash advances or new purchases. To pay a balance down, use the credit card payoff calculator . Is there a 10% credit card interest cap? No, a 10% credit card interest cap is not federal law. Proposals S. 381 and H.R. 1944 in the 119th Congress would cap consumer credit card rates at 10% until January 2031, per a Congressional Research Service (CRS) report updated March 10, 2026. S. 381 was introduced on February 4, 2025, and referred to Senate Banking, though current status after that is not confirmed here. How much would a 10% APR cap save on a $5,000 balance? A 10% cap saves $57.53 in interest over one 30-day billing cycle on a $5,000 balance, dropping the charge from $98.63 at 24% to $41.10. Our calculation assumes a 365-day year, simple interest, no payments, no new fees, and the card staying available at 10%. Auxiliary fees or lost access to credit if banks limit products could erase those savings. Sources We prioritize primary sources for rules, formulas, rates, limits, and definitions. schema.name: Credit Card Interest Calculator: Monthly Interest Cost
schema.description: Free credit card interest calculator. See one billing cycle's interest from your APR and average daily balance, and what a mid-cycle payment saves you.

mainEntity.name: How do I calculate my credit card interest?

acceptedAnswer.text: Divide your APR by the days in the year to get the daily rate, multiply it by your average daily balance, then multiply by the days in the billing cycle. Take a $5,000 balance at 24% APR. Over a 30-day cycle on a 365-day year, it is charged $98.63. Enter the figures from your own statement in the calculator above to get your number.

mainEntity.name: How much interest will a $5,000 balance cost in a month?

acceptedAnswer.text: At 24% APR, a $5,000 balance is charged $98.63 in one billing cycle. That assumes a 30-day cycle, a 365-day year and no payment during the cycle. On a 360-day basis, the same cycle costs $100.00. A different APR changes the figure, so enter your own rate above.

mainEntity.name: What is the daily periodic rate?

acceptedAnswer.text: The daily periodic rate is your APR divided by the days in the year. At 24% APR on a 365-day year, it is 0.0658% a day. On a 360-day year, the same APR gives 0.0667% a day.

mainEntity.name: What is the average daily balance?

acceptedAnswer.text: The average daily balance is the average of each day's balance across the billing cycle. A payment lowers it from the day the payment posts. Start with $5,000 and post a $1,000 payment on day 11. Across a 30-day cycle, the balance averages $4,333.33.

mainEntity.name: Does paying early in the billing cycle lower my interest?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. A payment lowers the balance for every remaining day in the cycle, so an earlier payment means a lower average daily balance. On a $5,000 balance at 24% APR, a $1,000 payment posting on day 11 drops the cycle's interest to $85.48. That is $13.15 less than the $98.63 charged with no payment.

mainEntity.name: Why is the effective annual rate higher than my APR?

acceptedAnswer.text: When interest compounds daily, each day's interest is added to the balance and then charged interest itself. At 24% APR, daily compounding over a 365-day year gives an effective annual rate of 27.11%. Simple interest on a flat $5,000 balance comes to $1,200 for the year.

mainEntity.name: Why does my statement show a slightly different amount?

acceptedAnswer.text: Some issuers divide the APR by 365 days and some by 360. On the $5,000 example, that difference is $98.63 versus $100.00 for one cycle. Issuers also differ in how they compound within a cycle and how they round, which can shift the statement amount slightly. Set the day-count input to the basis on your statement to get closer.

mainEntity.name: Does this calculator include a grace period or fees?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. It covers purchase interest only, with no grace period, fees, cash advances or new purchases. To pay a balance down, use the credit card payoff calculator.

mainEntity.name: Is there a 10% credit card interest cap?

acceptedAnswer.text: No, a 10% credit card interest cap is not federal law. Proposals S. 381 and H.R. 1944 in the 119th Congress would cap consumer credit card rates at 10% until January 2031, per a Congressional Research Service (CRS) report updated March 10, 2026. S. 381 was introduced on February 4, 2025, and referred to Senate Banking, though current status after that is not confirmed here.

mainEntity.name: How much would a 10% APR cap save on a $5,000 balance?

acceptedAnswer.text: A 10% cap saves $57.53 in interest over one 30-day billing cycle on a $5,000 balance, dropping the charge from $98.63 at 24% to $41.10. Our calculation assumes a 365-day year, simple interest, no payments, no new fees, and the card staying available at 10%. Auxiliary fees or lost access to credit if banks limit products could erase those savings.
